commands.title: Update & upgrade all packages
commands.description: Refreshes Termux package repositories and upgrades all installed packages to the latest available versions for better compatibility, security, and stability.
commands.howToUse: Run immediately after installing Termux. Paste the command into Termux and press Enter, then wait for the upgrade process to finish.
commands.whenToUse: Use it on a fresh Termux install, before installing development tools like Git or Node.js, and periodically to keep your environment updated and secure.
commands.tip: 💡 If asked about configuration file changes during the upgrade, press Enter to keep the currently installed version unless you know you need the new one.

commands.title: Grant storage permission
commands.description: Requests permission for Termux to access your Android device storage and creates convenient storage shortcuts such as Downloads, Pictures, Music, and shared internal storage.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux and tap 'Allow' when the Android permission prompt appears. After approval, access shared files through paths like ~/storage/shared/ and ~/storage/downloads/.
commands.whenToUse: Run once after installing Termux or whenever storage access has been revoked. Required before working with files stored outside the Termux home directory.
commands.tip: 💡 This command is essential for accessing project files, downloads, and media files from Termux, Acode, and Android file manager apps.

commands.title: Install the full dev toolkit
commands.code: pkg install git nodejs python openssh curl wget nano zip unzip -y
commands.description: Installs a complete development toolkit including Git, Node.js, npm, Python, OpenSSH, curl, wget, nano, zip, and unzip, providing the essential tools needed for web development, scripting, automation, and version control.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux and wait for all packages to download and install automatically. An internet connection is required during installation.
commands.whenToUse: Use during the initial setup of a fresh Termux environment after updating packages and granting storage permissions. It serves as a solid foundation for most development workflows.
commands.tip: 💡 Running a single installation command saves time and ensures all commonly used development tools are available before starting projects.

commands.title: Create your dev workspace
commands.description: Creates a dedicated development workspace and moves you into it, helping keep all projects organised in a single, consistent location.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux. The folder structure will be created automatically if it does not already exist, and your current directory will change to ~/dev/projects.
commands.whenToUse: Use after completing your initial Termux setup. Store all new projects, Git repositories, experiments, and learning projects inside this workspace for better organisation.
commands.tip: 💡 Keeping every project under ~/dev/projects makes navigation, backups, Git management, and project discovery much easier as your portfolio grows.

commands.title: Show Termux environment info
commands.description: Displays detailed information about your Termux installation, including the Termux version, Android version, device architecture, enabled repositories, and installed package statistics.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux and review the generated report displayed in the terminal.
commands.whenToUse: Use when troubleshooting issues, reporting bugs, verifying your environment, or sharing system information for technical support.
commands.tip: 💡 Include the output of this command when asking for help with Termux-related problems, as it provides useful diagnostic information.

commands.title: List all installed packages
commands.description: Lists all packages currently installed in your Termux environment along with their installed versions.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux to display a complete list of installed packages and their version numbers.
commands.whenToUse: Use when auditing your environment, checking whether a package is already installed, or reviewing your development setup before making changes.
commands.tip: 💡 Combine this command with search tools such as grep to quickly find specific packages in large installations.

commands.title: Install a package
commands.description: Installs a package from the Termux repositories. The -y flag automatically confirms installation prompts, allowing the process to complete without additional input.
commands.howToUse: Replace package-name with the desired package, such as git, nodejs, python, php, vim, ffmpeg, or mariadb, then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use whenever you need to add a new development tool, programming language runtime, utility, or command-line application to your Termux environment.
commands.tip: 💡 If you're unsure of the exact package name, use pkg search keyword first to find the correct package.

commands.title: Remove a package
commands.description: Removes an installed package from your Termux environment and frees up storage space on your device.
commands.howToUse: Replace package-name with the name of the package you want to remove, then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when a package is no longer needed, is causing conflicts, or when you want to reclaim storage space on your device.
commands.tip: 💡 Review installed packages before removal to avoid accidentally uninstalling tools that other projects depend on.

commands.title: Search for a package
commands.description: Searches the Termux package repositories for packages whose names or descriptions match a specified keyword.
commands.howToUse: Replace keyword with a relevant search term such as java, python, database, http, image, or editor, then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you do not know the exact package name, want to discover available tools, or need to find alternatives for a specific task.
commands.tip: 💡 Partial keywords work well, so broad searches can help you discover useful packages you may not have known existed.

commands.title: Go to home directory
commands.description: Navigates directly to your Termux home directory, which serves as the default starting location for your files, projects, and personal configuration data.
commands.howToUse: Run the command from any location in the terminal to instantly return to your home directory. You can also use a plain 'cd' command for the same result.
commands.whenToUse: Use whenever you are deep inside nested folders and want to quickly return to your main workspace or start navigating from a known location.
commands.tip: 💡 The '~' symbol is a shortcut that always points to your home directory, making it one of the most commonly used navigation shortcuts in Linux and Termux.

commands.title: List files with full details
commands.description: Lists all files and folders in the current directory, including hidden items, while displaying permissions, ownership, file sizes in a human-readable format, and modification dates.
commands.howToUse: Run the command inside any directory to view a detailed breakdown of its contents. Hidden files that normally start with a dot (.) will also be displayed.
commands.whenToUse: Use before creating, deleting, moving, or editing files to understand the current directory structure and verify that the files you need are present.
commands.tip: 💡 Useful variations include 'ls' for a simple listing, 'ls -la' for detailed information with hidden files, and 'ls -lt' to sort files by most recent modification time.

commands.title: Print current directory path
commands.description: Displays the full absolute path of your current working directory, showing exactly where you are in the filesystem.
commands.howToUse: Run the command from any directory in Termux to print the complete path of your current location.
commands.whenToUse: Use before running file operations, executing scripts, cloning repositories, or performing destructive commands to verify that you are working in the correct directory.
commands.tip: 💡 If you're ever unsure where a command is being executed, run 'pwd' first to avoid accidentally modifying files in the wrong location.

commands.title: Create nested project structure
commands.description: Creates a complete project directory structure in a single command, including common folders for source code, public assets, configuration files, tests, and utility scripts.
commands.howToUse: Run the command as provided to create the example project structure. Replace 'my-app' with your preferred project name and modify the folder list if your project requires a different layout.
commands.whenToUse: Use when starting a new project and you want to quickly scaffold an organised folder structure without relying on a framework or project generator.
commands.tip: 💡 Brace expansion lets you create multiple directories at once, saving time and helping maintain a consistent project structure across all your applications.

commands.title: Remove a folder and all contents
commands.description: Permanently deletes a directory and all files, subdirectories, and contents inside it without moving them to a recycle bin.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'folder-name' with the target directory and run the command. Verify the folder name and current location using 'pwd' and 'ls -lah' before executing.
commands.whenToUse: Use when removing old projects, deleting build directories such as node_modules, clearing temporary files, or cleaning up folders that are no longer needed.
commands.tip: ⚠️ This action cannot be undone. Never run 'rm -rf ~' or 'rm -rf /'. Always double-check the target folder before pressing Enter, as all contents will be permanently deleted.

commands.title: Create empty files
commands.description: Creates one or more empty files in the current directory. If a file already exists, its modification timestamp is updated without affecting its contents.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to create the example files, or replace the filenames with your own. Multiple files can be created at once by separating their names with spaces.
commands.whenToUse: Use when starting a new project, creating configuration files, scaffolding frontend assets, or preparing scripts that you plan to edit in Acode or another editor.
commands.tip: 💡 You can create an entire set of starter files in one command, making it a quick way to scaffold a project structure before writing any code.

commands.title: Create a file with content
commands.description: Creates a file and writes content to it in a single command. If the file already exists, the '>' operator overwrites its contents with the new text.
commands.howToUse: Replace the example text and filename with your own content and target file. Use '>' to create or overwrite a file, or use '>>' to append content to the end of an existing file.
commands.whenToUse: Use when creating configuration files, generating quick script templates, adding values to environment files, or writing simple content directly from the terminal without opening an editor.
commands.tip: 💡 Be careful when using the '>' operator because it replaces all existing file contents. Use '>>' when you want to add new content without removing what's already there.

commands.title: Copy a file or directory
commands.code:
cp source.js destination.js
cp -r src/ src-backup/
commands.description: Copies files or entire directories from one location to another. Use the '-r' flag when copying directories so that all nested files and folders are included.
commands.howToUse: Use 'cp source.js destination.js' to copy a file. Use 'cp -r source-folder/ destination-folder/' to copy a directory and all its contents. Replace the example names with your own paths and filenames.
commands.whenToUse: Use when creating backups, duplicating files before making changes, copying project templates, or preserving a working version of a directory before refactoring.
commands.tip: 💡 A common workflow is 'cp .env.example .env' to create a local configuration file from a template without modifying the original example file.

commands.title: Move or rename a file
commands.code:
mv old-name.js new-name.js
mv component.jsx src/components/
commands.description: Moves files or directories to a new location, or renames them without changing their contents. The same command is used for both moving and renaming operations.
commands.howToUse: Use 'mv old-name.js new-name.js' to rename a file. Use 'mv file-name destination-folder/' to move a file into another directory. Replace the example paths and filenames with your own.
commands.whenToUse: Use when reorganising project folders, renaming files or components, moving assets into dedicated directories, or restructuring an application as it grows.
commands.tip: 💡 If the destination file already exists, it may be overwritten without warning. Always verify the target path and filename before running the command.

commands.title: Delete a file
commands.code:
rm filename.js
rm -i filename.js # with confirmation prompt
commands.description: Permanently deletes a file from the filesystem. Deleted files are not moved to a recycle bin and cannot be easily recovered.
commands.howToUse: Use 'rm filename.js' to delete a file immediately. Use 'rm -i filename.js' to display a confirmation prompt before deletion. Replace the example filename with the file you want to remove.
commands.whenToUse: Use when removing obsolete files, generated build artifacts, temporary files, logs, or other project files that are no longer needed.
commands.tip: 💡 Prefer 'rm -i' when deleting important files to reduce the risk of accidental data loss. Use 'ls -lah' first if you're unsure which file you're about to remove.

commands.title: Print full file contents
commands.description: Displays the entire contents of a file directly in the terminal, making it easy to quickly inspect text files without opening an editor.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'filename.js' with the path to the file you want to view and run the command. The file contents will be printed to the terminal from beginning to end.
commands.whenToUse: Use when checking configuration files, package.json, .gitignore, .env examples, scripts, logs, or other small text files that can be comfortably viewed on a single terminal screen.
commands.tip: 💡 For large files, use commands like 'head', 'tail', or 'less' instead of 'cat' to avoid flooding the terminal with excessive output.

commands.title: View first N lines
commands.description: Displays the first N lines of a file, allowing you to quickly preview its contents without reading the entire file. If no line count is specified, the default is 10 lines.
commands.howToUse: Replace '20' with the number of lines you want to view and replace 'server.js' with your target file. Run the command to print only the beginning portion of the file.
commands.whenToUse: Use when inspecting large files, checking import statements, reviewing configuration headers, previewing datasets, or examining the beginning of log files.
commands.tip: 💡 Use 'head filename.js' for the default 10-line preview, or increase the number when you need more context without displaying the entire file.

commands.title: View last N lines + follow mode
commands.code:
tail -50 app.log
# Live follow — shows new lines as written:
tail -f app.log
commands.description: Displays the last N lines of a file and can optionally follow the file in real time, showing new content as it is added. This is especially useful for monitoring logs and live system output.
commands.howToUse: Use 'tail -50 app.log' to view the last 50 lines of a file. Use 'tail -f app.log' to continuously stream new lines as they are written. Press Ctrl+C to stop follow mode.
commands.whenToUse: Use when monitoring server logs, debugging runtime errors, watching build processes, or tracking real-time application output.
commands.tip: 💡 Follow mode (-f) is one of the most powerful debugging tools for backend development because it lets you see issues as they happen in real time.

commands.title: Search text inside files (grep)
commands.code:
grep -rn "TODO" ./src
grep -ri "console.log" . # case-insensitive
grep -rl "import React" . # filenames only
commands.description: Searches for specific text patterns inside files and directories recursively. It can show matching lines, line numbers, or just filenames depending on the flags used.
commands.howToUse: Run the command with a search keyword and target directory. Use '-r' for recursive search, '-n' to show line numbers, '-i' for case-insensitive search, and '-l' to return only filenames containing matches.
commands.whenToUse: Use when finding TODO comments, debugging codebases, locating function usage, auditing console.log statements before production, or tracking where specific imports or variables are used.
commands.tip: 💡 Combine grep with specific folders (like ./src) to improve performance and reduce noise in large projects.

commands.title: Count lines / words / bytes
commands.code:
wc -l filename.js
wc -l src/*.js # multiple files with total
commands.description: Counts lines, words, or bytes in files. The '-l' option counts lines, '-w' counts words, and '-c' counts bytes. It also supports multiple files and displays a total summary.
commands.howToUse: Run 'wc -l filename.js' to count lines in a single file, or use wildcards like 'wc -l src/*.js' to analyze multiple files at once. Replace flags depending on whether you need lines, words, or bytes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when analyzing codebase size, counting dataset rows, measuring file growth, or getting quick statistics about files in a project.
commands.tip: 💡 Combine with wildcards to quickly evaluate the scale of your entire project folder without opening files manually.

commands.title: Install Termux
commands.code: # Download Termux from F-Droid (NOT Google Play)
commands.description: Termux is an Android terminal emulator and Linux environment. The Google Play version is outdated and not recommended, so installation should be done from trusted sources like F-Droid or GitHub releases.
commands.howToUse: Open your browser, go to f-droid.org, search for 'Termux', download and install the app, then launch it to automatically initialize the environment setup.
commands.whenToUse: Use this as the very first step before any development setup, Git usage, or package installation on Android.
commands.tip: 💡 Always prefer F-Droid or official GitHub releases to ensure you get the latest secure version of Termux with full package support.

commands.title: Install Acode Editor
commands.code: # Download Acode from Google Play Store
commands.description: Acode is a powerful Android code editor with syntax highlighting, file management, and extensions support. It acts as a lightweight VS Code alternative for mobile development.
commands.howToUse: Open Google Play Store, search for 'Acode - code editor', install it, launch the app, and grant storage permissions when prompted.
commands.whenToUse: Use when setting up your Android development environment alongside Termux for writing and editing code with a proper GUI editor.
commands.tip: 💡 Use Acode for editing files and Termux for running commands — this combo gives you a full mobile development workflow.

commands.title: Update Termux packages
commands.description: Updates all installed Termux packages to their latest versions, ensuring stability, security, and compatibility before installing new tools.
commands.howToUse: Open Termux, paste the command, and press Enter. Wait for the update process to complete.
commands.whenToUse: Use immediately after installing Termux and periodically to keep your environment up to date.
commands.tip: 💡 If prompted about configuration changes, press Enter to keep default versions unless you specifically need changes.

commands.title: Install Git in Termux
commands.description: Installs Git version control system, enabling repository cloning, commits, and GitHub integration inside Termux.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux and wait for Git installation to complete.
commands.whenToUse: Use after updating Termux packages when setting up a new development environment.
commands.tip: 💡 Git is the backbone of modern development workflows — install it early in every setup.

commands.title: Install essential tools
commands.code: pkg install openssh curl wget nano -y
commands.description: Installs essential command-line tools including SSH for authentication, curl and wget for downloads, and nano for simple file editing.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux to install all tools in one step.
commands.whenToUse: Use after installing Git to complete your basic development toolkit.
commands.tip: 💡 These tools are required for most GitHub workflows, API testing, and remote server access.

commands.title: Install Node.js (optional)
commands.description: Installs Node.js and npm for JavaScript backend development and tooling.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux to install Node.js and npm.
commands.whenToUse: Use when building JavaScript projects such as React apps, APIs, or CLI tools.
commands.tip: 💡 Node.js enables full-stack JavaScript development directly on your phone.

commands.title: Install Python (optional)
commands.description: Installs Python 3 for scripting, automation, and backend development tasks.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux to install Python.
commands.whenToUse: Use when working on automation scripts, data processing, or Python-based projects.
commands.tip: 💡 Python is great for quick automation scripts and backend prototyping.

commands.title: Grant Termux storage access
commands.description: Grants Termux access to Android shared storage and creates shortcuts for easy file access.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux and tap 'Allow' when the permission popup appears.
commands.whenToUse: Use immediately after installing Termux to enable file sharing between apps.
commands.tip: 💡 Essential for accessing files between Termux, Acode, and file manager apps.

commands.title: Create a projects folder
commands.description: Creates a shared projects directory accessible from both Termux and Acode for unified file management.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to create and enter the projects directory automatically.
commands.whenToUse: Use after granting storage access to organize all your development projects in one location.
commands.tip: 💡 Keeping all projects in one shared folder improves workflow consistency across tools.

commands.title: Set Termux as Acode terminal
commands.code: # In Acode: Settings → App → Terminal → Choose Termux
commands.description: Connects Acode to Termux so you can run terminal commands directly from the editor.
commands.howToUse: Open Acode, go to Settings, find Terminal settings, and select Termux as the default terminal app.
commands.whenToUse: Use after installing both Acode and Termux to streamline development workflow.
commands.tip: 💡 This integration makes mobile development feel closer to a desktop VS Code setup.

commands.title: Verify Git installation
commands.description: Checks if Git is installed correctly and displays the installed version.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux and verify that a Git version number is displayed.
commands.whenToUse: Use after installing Git to confirm proper installation.
commands.tip: 💡 If no version appears, Git installation likely failed and should be reinstalled.

commands.title: Set your name
commands.description: Sets the global Git username used in all commit history.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'Your Name' with your actual name or GitHub username and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use during initial Git configuration before making any commits.
commands.tip: 💡 This name will appear publicly on all your Git commits.

commands.title: Set your email
commands.description: Sets the email address associated with your Git commits.
commands.howToUse: Replace the placeholder email with your GitHub-registered email and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use immediately after setting your Git username.
commands.tip: 💡 Use the same email linked to your GitHub account for proper commit attribution.

commands.title: Set default text editor
commands.description: Defines the default text editor Git uses for commit messages and edits.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to set nano as your default Git editor.
commands.whenToUse: Use when configuring Git for the first time or switching editors.
commands.tip: 💡 Nano is beginner-friendly and easier to use than Vim for most developers.

commands.title: View all your Git config
commands.description: Displays all Git configuration values currently set for the system, global user, and local repository.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in Termux to view all Git settings in one output.
commands.whenToUse: Use when troubleshooting Git identity issues, verifying setup, or confirming configuration changes.
commands.tip: 💡 Helps quickly confirm whether your user.name and user.email are correctly set.

commands.title: Generate SSH key pair
commands.description: Creates a secure Ed25519 SSH key pair used for authenticating with GitHub without passwords.
commands.howToUse: Run the command, press Enter to accept default file location, and press Enter again when asked for a passphrase (optional).
commands.whenToUse: Use once per device when setting up secure GitHub authentication.
commands.tip: 💡 Ed25519 is modern, fast, and more secure than older RSA keys.

commands.title: Display your public SSH key
commands.description: Displays your public SSH key so it can be copied and added to GitHub.
commands.howToUse: Run the command and copy the full output starting with 'ssh-ed25519', then paste it into GitHub SSH settings.
commands.whenToUse: Use after generating an SSH key and before attempting GitHub SSH authentication.
commands.tip: 💡 Only share the public key, never the private key.

commands.title: Initialize a new repository
commands.description: Initializes a new Git repository by creating a .git folder to track version history.
commands.howToUse: Navigate into your project folder and run the command to initialize Git tracking.
commands.whenToUse: Use when starting a brand-new project before making your first commit.
commands.tip: 💡 Always run inside your project folder, not in home or system directories.

commands.title: Set default branch to main
commands.description: Sets 'main' as the default branch name for all new Git repositories.
commands.howToUse: Run once globally in Termux to configure default branch naming.
commands.whenToUse: Use during initial Git setup to align with modern GitHub standards.
commands.tip: 💡 Prevents the old 'master' branch from being created in new repositories.

commands.title: Set nano as default editor
commands.description: Sets nano as the default text editor used by Git for commit messages and edits.
commands.howToUse: Run once to configure Git to use nano instead of vim.
commands.whenToUse: Use during initial setup if you prefer a simpler editor in Termux.
commands.tip: 💡 Nano is beginner-friendly and avoids vim complexity.

commands.title: Enable colorful output
commands.description: Enables colored Git output for better readability of changes and status messages.
commands.howToUse: Run once globally to enable colorized Git output.
commands.whenToUse: Use during initial Git setup to improve readability of terminal output.
commands.tip: 💡 Makes diffs, branches, and status much easier to read.

commands.title: Set pull to rebase
commands.description: Configures Git pull to use rebase instead of merge for a cleaner commit history.
commands.howToUse: Run once globally to change default pull behavior.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want a linear commit history without merge commits.
commands.tip: 💡 Helps keep project history clean and easier to read.

commands.title: Set push to current branch
commands.description: Automatically pushes the current branch to a remote branch with the same name.
commands.howToUse: Run once globally to simplify push commands.
commands.whenToUse: Use to avoid manually specifying branch names during pushes.
commands.tip: 💡 Saves time when working with multiple branches.

commands.title: Enable credential caching
commands.description: Caches Git credentials temporarily to avoid repeated login prompts.
commands.howToUse: Run once to enable temporary credential storage for Git operations.
commands.whenToUse: Use when working with HTTPS GitHub repositories to reduce login frequency.
commands.tip: 💡 Credentials are cached for 1 hour by default (3600 seconds).

commands.title: List all your config
commands.description: Displays all Git configuration values along with their source files.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to see all Git configs and where they are defined.
commands.whenToUse: Use when debugging configuration issues or verifying setup hierarchy.
commands.tip: 💡 Helps identify whether settings come from global or local config.

commands.title: Check a specific setting
commands.description: Retrieves the value of a specific Git configuration key.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'user.name' with any config key you want to inspect.
commands.whenToUse: Use when verifying a single configuration value.
commands.tip: 💡 Faster than listing all configs when checking one value.

commands.title: Create a .gitignore
commands.description: Creates a .gitignore file to exclude unnecessary or sensitive files from Git tracking.
commands.howToUse: Run inside your project folder to generate a basic .gitignore file.
commands.whenToUse: Use at the start of every project before making commits.
commands.tip: 💡 Prevents clutter and keeps repositories clean and secure.

commands.title: Generate SSH key
commands.description: Generates an SSH key pair for secure authentication with GitHub.
commands.howToUse: Run the command, press Enter for defaults, and skip passphrase if desired.
commands.whenToUse: Use when setting up GitHub SSH authentication.
commands.tip: 💡 Required for passwordless Git operations over SSH.

commands.title: Display your public key
commands.description: Displays the public SSH key for copying into GitHub.
commands.howToUse: Run the command and copy the full output starting with ssh-ed25519.
commands.whenToUse: Use after generating SSH keys to register them on GitHub.
commands.tip: 💡 Never share your private key.

commands.title: Start SSH agent
commands.description: Starts the SSH agent and adds your private key for authentication.
commands.howToUse: Run the command each time you open Termux unless auto-start is configured.
commands.whenToUse: Use after generating SSH keys to enable authentication.
commands.tip: 💡 Keeps your SSH key active during the session.

commands.title: Test GitHub connection
commands.description: Tests whether SSH authentication with GitHub is working correctly.
commands.howToUse: Run the command and confirm connection when prompted.
commands.whenToUse: Use after adding SSH key to GitHub.
commands.tip: 💡 A successful test confirms your SSH setup is correct.

commands.title: Auto-start SSH agent
commands.description: Automatically starts SSH agent when Termux launches.
commands.howToUse: Run once to append the command to your shell configuration.
commands.whenToUse: Use after verifying SSH works correctly.
commands.tip: 💡 Automates SSH setup for every session.

commands.title: Fix SSH permissions
commands.description: Fixes SSH file permissions to meet security requirements.
commands.howToUse: Run the command if SSH refuses to work due to permission issues.
commands.whenToUse: Use when SSH keys are rejected or warnings appear.
commands.tip: 💡 Incorrect permissions are a common cause of SSH failure.

commands.title: Initialize new repo
commands.description: Initializes a new Git repository in the current directory.
commands.howToUse: Run inside your project folder to start version control.
commands.whenToUse: Use when starting a new project from scratch.
commands.tip: 💡 Always ensure you're in the correct folder before running.

commands.title: Init with main branch
commands.description: Initializes a new Git repository and explicitly sets the default branch name to 'main' instead of the older default 'master'.
commands.howToUse: Run inside a new project folder to create a Git repository with 'main' as the starting branch.
commands.whenToUse: Use when starting any new project to ensure modern GitHub-compatible branch naming.
commands.tip: 💡 Always prefer this over plain 'git init' to avoid legacy branch naming issues.

commands.title: Check status
commands.description: Displays the current state of your working directory, showing modified, staged, and untracked files.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in your project folder to see Git's view of your current changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use before staging, committing, or whenever you're unsure what Git is tracking.
commands.tip: 💡 Red files are untracked or modified, green files are staged and ready to commit.

commands.title: Short status
commands.description: Provides a compact, single-line summary of repository status and current branch.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to get a concise overview of changes and branch state.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want a quick status check without verbose output.
commands.tip: 💡 Ideal for fast workflow checks in active development.

commands.title: Stage a specific file
commands.description: Adds a single file to the staging area, preparing it for commit.
commands.howToUse: Replace the file path with the actual file you want to stage, then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to commit only selected changes instead of everything.
commands.tip: 💡 Staging lets you control exactly what goes into each commit.

commands.title: Stage multiple files
commands.description: Stages multiple specific files in a single command.
commands.howToUse: List all filenames separated by spaces and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when grouping related changes into a single commit.
commands.tip: 💡 Useful for batching logically related changes.

commands.title: Stage everything
commands.description: Stages all changes in the current directory, including new, modified, and deleted files.
commands.howToUse: Run the command inside your project folder, then verify with 'git status'.
commands.whenToUse: Use when all current changes should be included in the next commit.
commands.tip: 💡 Be careful — this includes everything in the directory.

commands.title: Stage all tracked files
commands.description: Stages only modifications and deletions of files already tracked by Git, excluding new files.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to stage updates to existing tracked files only.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to avoid accidentally adding new untracked files.
commands.tip: 💡 Great for controlled commits in large projects.

commands.title: Stage interactively
commands.description: Allows selective staging of changes in chunks, giving full control over what gets committed.
commands.howToUse: Run the command and respond to prompts (y = stage, n = skip, q = quit).
commands.whenToUse: Use when a file contains multiple unrelated changes that should be split into separate commits.
commands.tip: 💡 Helps maintain clean and atomic commits.

commands.title: Commit with message
commands.description: Creates a commit with a message describing the changes made.
commands.howToUse: Stage your files first, then run the command with a meaningful commit message.
commands.whenToUse: Use after staging changes to save a snapshot of your work.
commands.tip: 💡 Use clear commit messages like 'feat:', 'fix:', or 'chore:'.

commands.title: Stage + commit in one step
commands.description: Stages and commits all modified tracked files in one command, skipping untracked files.
commands.howToUse: Run the command with a commit message to quickly save changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use for fast commits when working with already tracked files.
commands.tip: 💡 Does NOT include new files — only modified tracked ones.

commands.title: Amend last commit
commands.description: Updates the previous commit by adding newly staged changes without changing the commit message.
commands.howToUse: Stage new changes first, then run the command to modify the last commit.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you forgot to include files in your last commit.
commands.tip: 💡 This rewrites history — avoid using after pushing to remote.

commands.title: Change last commit message
commands.description: Modifies the most recent commit message.
commands.howToUse: Run the command with a new message to replace the last commit message.
commands.whenToUse: Use when correcting typos or improving commit messages.
commands.tip: 💡 Also rewrites history — use carefully if already pushed.

commands.title: Unstage a file
commands.description: Removes a file from the staging area without deleting its changes.
commands.howToUse: Replace the file path with the staged file you want to unstage.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you accidentally staged a file you don't want in the next commit.
commands.tip: 💡 Safe operation — does not delete any work.

commands.title: Discard file changes
commands.description: Reverts a file back to its last committed state, discarding all local changes.
commands.howToUse: Run the command with the target file path to undo changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to completely undo unwanted edits.
commands.tip: ⚠️ This permanently deletes uncommitted changes.

commands.title: See what you changed
commands.description: Shows line-by-line differences between working directory and last commit.
commands.howToUse: Run the command before staging to review changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use to inspect modifications before adding them to staging.
commands.tip: 💡 Green = additions, red = deletions.

commands.title: See what's staged
commands.description: Shows changes that have been staged and will be included in the next commit.
commands.howToUse: Run after staging files to verify what will be committed.
commands.whenToUse: Use before committing to confirm final changes.
commands.tip: 💡 Final checkpoint before committing.

commands.title: List local branches
commands.description: Displays all local branches in the repository and highlights the current branch.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in a Git repository to list branches.
commands.whenToUse: Use when checking which branch you're currently working on.
commands.tip: 💡 The active branch is marked with *.

commands.title: List all branches
commands.description: Shows both local and remote-tracking branches.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to view all available branches.
commands.whenToUse: Use when inspecting remote branches from GitHub.
commands.tip: 💡 Useful for understanding full repository structure.

commands.title: Create + switch to new branch
commands.description: Creates a new branch from the current state and immediately switches to it.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'feature/login' with a descriptive branch name like 'feature/auth' or 'fix/navbar-bug', then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when starting a new feature, bug fix, or experiment that should be isolated from main code.
commands.tip: 💡 Use descriptive branch names like feature/, fix/, or chore/ for better project organization.

commands.title: Switch to existing branch
commands.description: Switches your working directory to an existing branch.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'main' with the branch you want to switch to and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when moving between different features or returning to main branch.
commands.tip: 💡 Ensure you commit or stash changes before switching branches.

commands.title: Switch to previous branch
commands.description: Quickly toggles back to the previously checked-out branch.
commands.howToUse: Run the command without arguments to return to the last branch you were on.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you temporarily switch branches and want to return quickly.
commands.tip: 💡 Works like a back button between branches.

commands.title: Create branch from specific commit
commands.description: Creates a new branch starting from a specific commit hash.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'abc1234' with the commit hash and 'hotfix/bug123' with your branch name.
commands.whenToUse: Use when fixing issues based on older commits in history.
commands.tip: 💡 Useful for hotfixing production bugs.

commands.title: Rename current branch
commands.description: Renames the branch you are currently on.
commands.howToUse: Run the command and replace 'new-name' with your desired branch name.
commands.whenToUse: Use when correcting or improving branch naming.
commands.tip: 💡 Keep branch names meaningful and consistent.

commands.title: Rename any branch
commands.description: Renames a branch without needing to be currently on it.
commands.howToUse: Replace old and new branch names and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when refactoring branch names across the project.
commands.tip: 💡 Helps maintain clean and readable branch history.

commands.title: Delete merged branch
commands.description: Deletes a branch only if it has been fully merged into another branch.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'feature/login' with the branch you want to delete.
commands.whenToUse: Use after merging feature branches into main to clean up.
commands.tip: 💡 Safe deletion — Git prevents accidental loss of unmerged work.

commands.title: Force-delete branch
commands.description: Forcibly deletes a branch even if it contains unmerged changes.
commands.howToUse: Replace branch name and run the command carefully.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you are sure the branch and its changes are no longer needed.
commands.tip: ⚠️ This can permanently delete unmerged work.

commands.title: Delete remote branch
commands.description: Removes a branch from the remote repository (e.g., GitHub).
commands.howToUse: Replace 'feature/login' with the remote branch name and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use after merging pull requests to clean up remote branches.
commands.tip: 💡 Does not delete local branch — only affects GitHub.

commands.title: Check out detached commit
commands.description: Checks out a specific commit without being on any branch (detached HEAD state).
commands.howToUse: Replace commit hash and run the command to inspect historical code.
commands.whenToUse: Use when reviewing old versions of the codebase.
commands.tip: 💡 Avoid making changes here unless you create a new branch.

commands.title: Add remote (SSH)
commands.description: Connects your local repository to a remote GitHub repository using SSH.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'user/repo' with your GitHub repository path and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use after initializing a local repo when linking it to GitHub.
commands.tip: 💡 SSH setup allows passwordless Git operations.

commands.title: Add remote (HTTPS)
commands.description: Connects your local repository to a GitHub repository using HTTPS.
commands.howToUse: Replace the URL with your GitHub repo link, then run the command inside your project folder.
commands.whenToUse: Use when setting up a repository without SSH authentication configured.
commands.tip: 💡 HTTPS requires a personal access token for authentication instead of a password.

commands.title: List remotes
commands.description: Displays all configured remote repositories and their fetch/push URLs.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in your repo to inspect connected remotes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when verifying which GitHub repository your project is linked to.
commands.tip: 💡 Always check remotes before pushing to avoid wrong repository uploads.

commands.title: Change remote URL
commands.description: Updates the URL of an existing remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Replace the URL with the new remote (SSH or HTTPS) and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when switching authentication methods or repository location.
commands.tip: 💡 Common when migrating from HTTPS to SSH.

commands.title: Remove a remote
commands.description: Disconnects the local repository from a remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to remove the 'origin' remote.
commands.whenToUse: Use when changing project repositories or resetting remote configuration.
commands.tip: 💡 Does not delete your local project — only removes the link.

commands.title: Fetch updates
commands.description: Downloads updates from the remote repository without modifying your working files.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to fetch latest commits from GitHub.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to inspect remote changes before merging.
commands.tip: 💡 Safe operation — it does not change your local code.

commands.title: Fetch + cleanup
commands.description: Fetches updates and removes references to deleted remote branches.
commands.howToUse: Run the command periodically to clean up stale branch references.
commands.whenToUse: Use when remote branches have been deleted on GitHub.
commands.tip: 💡 Keeps your local branch list clean and accurate.

commands.title: Pull (fetch + merge)
commands.description: Fetches remote changes and merges them into your current branch.
commands.howToUse: Ensure you're on the correct branch, then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use to sync your local branch with the latest remote updates.
commands.tip: 💡 Always commit or stash changes before pulling.

commands.title: Pull with rebase
commands.description: Fetches remote changes and re-applies your local commits on top of them.
commands.howToUse: Run the command instead of regular pull for cleaner history.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want a linear commit history without merge commits.
commands.tip: 💡 Preferred for teams that enforce clean Git history.

commands.title: Push current branch
commands.description: Uploads your local commits to the remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Run the command after committing your changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to publish your work to GitHub.
commands.tip: 💡 Only works if the branch is already tracked remotely.

commands.title: Push + set upstream
commands.description: Pushes the branch and sets it to track the remote branch.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'main' with your branch name and run once per branch.
commands.whenToUse: Use when pushing a new branch to GitHub for the first time.
commands.tip: 💡 After this, you can use plain 'git push' and 'git pull'.

commands.title: Push new branch shortcut
commands.description: Pushes the current branch and sets upstream tracking automatically.
commands.howToUse: Run the command while on the branch you want to push.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you don't want to type the branch name manually.
commands.tip: 💡 HEAD always refers to your current branch.

commands.title: Safe force-push
commands.description: Force-pushes changes but prevents overwriting remote work unintentionally.
commands.howToUse: Run after rebasing or amending commits that were already pushed.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you need to rewrite remote history safely.
commands.tip: 💡 Safer alternative to --force push.

commands.title: Merge branch into current
commands.description: Combines changes from another branch into your current branch.
commands.howToUse: Switch to the target branch first, then run the merge command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when completing a feature and integrating it into main.
commands.tip: 💡 Creates a merge commit unless fast-forward is possible.

commands.title: Merge with explicit commit
commands.description: Forces Git to create a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible.
commands.howToUse: Run the command while on the target branch.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to preserve branch history explicitly.
commands.tip: 💡 Helps maintain clear feature branch history.

commands.title: Squash merge
commands.description: Combines all commits from a branch into a single staged change.
commands.howToUse: Run command, then commit manually with a clean message.
commands.whenToUse: Use when feature branch has messy commit history.
commands.tip: 💡 Produces a clean single commit on main.

commands.title: Abort a merge
commands.description: Cancels an ongoing merge and restores previous state.
commands.howToUse: Run during a merge conflict you want to cancel.
commands.whenToUse: Use when merge conflicts become too complex to resolve.
commands.tip: 💡 Safe way to exit a failed merge.

commands.title: Rebase onto main
commands.description: Reapplies your branch commits on top of the latest main branch.
commands.howToUse: Run while on your feature branch.
commands.whenToUse: Use to keep your branch updated with main changes.
commands.tip: 💡 Creates clean linear commit history.

commands.title: Interactive rebase
commands.description: Lets you modify, reorder, squash, or delete recent commits interactively.
commands.howToUse: Run and choose actions (pick, squash, drop) in the editor.
commands.whenToUse: Use before pushing to clean up commit history.
commands.tip: 💡 Powerful tool — use carefully to avoid rewriting shared history.

commands.title: Continue rebase after conflict
commands.description: Continues a rebase after resolving conflicts.
commands.howToUse: Resolve conflicts, stage files, then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use during a rebase process after fixing conflicts.
commands.tip: 💡 Ensures rebase progresses step by step.

commands.title: Abort rebase
commands.description: Cancels the rebase and restores the repository to its original state.
commands.howToUse: Run when a rebase becomes too complex or problematic.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to restart the rebase process.
commands.tip: 💡 Safe rollback option during rebase operations.

commands.title: Cherry-pick a commit
commands.description: Applies a specific commit from another branch directly onto your current branch.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'abc1234' with the commit hash (use 'git log --oneline' to find it), then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you need a single fix or feature from another branch without merging everything.
commands.tip: 💡 Great for hotfixes and selective feature adoption.

commands.title: Cherry-pick without committing
commands.description: Applies changes from a commit to your working directory without creating a commit automatically.
commands.howToUse: Run the command, then review and manually commit the changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to modify changes before committing them.
commands.tip: 💡 Gives full control over final commit content.

commands.title: Resolve merge conflicts
commands.code: # Open conflicted file in editor and resolve <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers
commands.description: Handles Git merge conflicts by manually choosing which code to keep when automatic merging fails.
commands.howToUse: Open conflicted files in Acode, remove conflict markers, then stage and continue merge or rebase.
commands.whenToUse: Use when Git reports CONFLICT during merge or rebase operations.
commands.tip: 💡 Always review carefully before staging resolved files.

commands.title: Pretty commit log
commands.description: Displays a compact visual representation of recent commits with branch structure.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in your repository to view recent commit history.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you need a quick visual overview of project history.
commands.tip: 💡 Best command for understanding branch relationships.

commands.title: Full log (detailed)
commands.description: Shows complete commit history including hash, author, date, and message.
commands.howToUse: Run the command and navigate using arrow keys; press 'q' to exit.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you need detailed commit inspection.
commands.tip: 💡 Combine with filters for advanced debugging.

commands.title: Log by author
commands.description: Filters commit history by author and time range.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'YourName' and adjust time range as needed.
commands.whenToUse: Use when reviewing your own contributions or team activity.
commands.tip: 💡 Great for tracking productivity or recent changes.

commands.title: Log for a specific file
commands.description: Shows full history of changes for a specific file, including diffs and renames.
commands.howToUse: Replace file path and run to trace file evolution.
commands.whenToUse: Use when debugging changes in a specific file.
commands.tip: 💡 --follow is useful for renamed files.

commands.title: Search commits by message
commands.description: Searches commit history for messages matching a keyword.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'login' with your search term and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when looking for commits related to a feature or bug.
commands.tip: 💡 Fast way to locate feature-related commits.

commands.title: Search commits by code change
commands.description: Finds commits where a specific string was added or removed in code.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'functionName' with the target string and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when tracking when a function or variable was introduced or removed.
commands.tip: 💡 Powerful for debugging breaking changes.

commands.title: Show a specific commit
commands.description: Displays detailed information and diff for a specific commit.
commands.howToUse: Replace commit hash and run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when inspecting exactly what a commit changed.
commands.tip: 💡 Essential for debugging regressions.

commands.title: Show unstaged changes
commands.description: Shows differences between working directory and staged/committed state.
commands.howToUse: Run before staging to review your changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when verifying modifications before adding them.
commands.tip: 💡 Red = removed, green = added.

commands.title: Show staged changes
commands.description: Shows differences that are staged and ready for commit.
commands.howToUse: Run after staging files to verify commit content.
commands.whenToUse: Use before committing to double-check staged changes.
commands.tip: 💡 Final safety check before commit.

commands.title: Compare two branches
commands.description: Shows differences between two branches to preview what changes will be introduced.
commands.howToUse: Replace branch names and run the command to compare their full differences.
commands.whenToUse: Use before merging or opening a pull request to review changes.
commands.tip: 💡 Always compare before merging to avoid unexpected changes.

commands.title: Who changed this line (blame)
commands.description: Shows who last modified each line of a file with commit details.
commands.howToUse: Replace file path and run the command to inspect line-by-line authorship.
commands.whenToUse: Use when debugging or investigating why a piece of code exists.
commands.tip: 💡 Great for tracking down when bugs were introduced.

commands.title: Reflog (safety net)
commands.description: Shows a complete history of all HEAD movements including commits, resets, and rebases.
commands.howToUse: Run the command to view past states of your repository.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you need to recover lost commits or undo destructive actions.
commands.tip: 💡 Acts as your ultimate undo history in Git.

commands.title: Show file at specific commit
commands.description: Displays the contents of a file as it existed at a specific commit.
commands.howToUse: Replace commit hash and file path, then run the command.
commands.whenToUse: Use when inspecting historical versions of a file.
commands.tip: 💡 Useful for debugging past behavior without checkout.

commands.title: Count commits per author
commands.description: Summarizes commits grouped by author and sorted by count.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in your repository to see contribution statistics.
commands.whenToUse: Use when analyzing team contributions or project activity.
commands.tip: 💡 Great for project analytics and reporting.

commands.title: Discard ALL changes
commands.description: Reverts all modified files back to their last committed state.
commands.howToUse: Run the command in your project root to reset working directory changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to completely discard all uncommitted work.
commands.tip: ⚠️ This permanently deletes all uncommitted changes.

commands.title: Unstage everything
commands.description: Removes all files from the staging area while keeping file changes.
commands.howToUse: Run the command after accidentally staging multiple files.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to reset staging without losing edits.
commands.tip: 💡 Safe operation — does not delete work.

commands.title: Delete untracked files (dry run)
commands.description: Shows which untracked files would be deleted without actually deleting them.
commands.howToUse: Run first to preview cleanup results before actual deletion.
commands.whenToUse: Use before cleaning up generated or unwanted files.
commands.tip: 💡 Always run this before git clean -fd.

commands.title: Delete untracked files
commands.description: Permanently deletes untracked files and directories from the working tree.
commands.howToUse: Run carefully in your project directory.
commands.whenToUse: Use when cleaning build artifacts or unwanted files.
commands.tip: ⚠️ This operation is irreversible.

commands.title: Revert a commit (safe)
commands.description: Creates a new commit that reverses the changes from a previous commit without rewriting history.
commands.howToUse: Replace commit hash and run the command to undo changes safely.
commands.whenToUse: Use on shared branches where history should not be rewritten.
commands.tip: 💡 Preferred over reset in collaborative environments.

commands.title: Soft reset (undo commit, keep staged)
commands.description: Moves HEAD back one commit while keeping changes staged.
commands.howToUse: Run to undo last commit but preserve staged changes.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you need to adjust the last commit before re-committing.
commands.tip: 💡 Safe way to redo your last commit.

commands.title: Mixed reset (undo commit, keep files)
commands.description: Moves HEAD back one commit and unstages changes while keeping them in working directory.
commands.howToUse: Run to undo last commit and re-stage selectively.
commands.whenToUse: Use when you want to reorganize staged changes.
commands.tip: 💡 Default reset mode.

commands.title: Hard reset (destroy everything)
commands.description: Resets repository to a previous commit and deletes all changes permanently.
commands.howToUse: Run carefully when you want to completely discard recent work.
commands.whenToUse: Use only when you are absolutely sure you want to lose changes.
commands.tip: ⚠️ Irreversible — deletes commits and file changes.

commands.title: Reset to match remote
commands.description: Forces local branch to match the remote repository exactly.
commands.howToUse: Run to sync local branch with GitHub state.
commands.whenToUse: Use when local repository is broken or out of sync.
commands.tip: ⚠️ Destroys all local changes and commits.

commands.title: Recover a deleted commit
commands.description: Restores your repository to a previous commit using the reflog history.
commands.howToUse: Run 'git reflog' first to find the commit hash you want to recover, then replace 'abc1234' with that hash and run the reset command inside the repository.
commands.whenToUse: After accidentally deleting commits, performing an unwanted reset, or needing to recover lost work from recent repository history.
commands.tip: Review the reflog carefully before resetting. This command discards your current working state and moves HEAD to the selected commit.

commands.title: Stash changes
commands.description: Temporarily saves your modified files and restores the working tree to the latest commit state.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the project folder and replace the message with something meaningful so the stash is easy to identify later.
commands.whenToUse: When you need to switch branches or pull changes but are not ready to commit your current work.
commands.tip: Use descriptive messages to make finding and restoring stashes easier.

commands.title: Stash including new files
commands.code: git stash push -u -m "wip: including new files"
commands.description: Saves both modified files and untracked files in a stash entry.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository and replace the message with a description of the work being saved.
commands.whenToUse: When your unfinished work includes newly created files that have not been added to Git yet.
commands.tip: The '-u' flag includes untracked files but does not include ignored files.

commands.title: Quick stash (no message)
commands.description: Temporarily saves your current changes using an automatically generated message.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository to quickly clean the working tree.
commands.whenToUse: When you need to switch context quickly and do not need a custom stash description.
commands.tip: Named stashes are easier to manage when multiple entries exist.

commands.title: List stashes
commands.description: Displays all saved stash entries and their messages.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository to view available stashes and their index numbers.
commands.whenToUse: Before applying, popping, or deleting a stash.
commands.tip: Use the stash index shown in the output when working with a specific stash entry.

commands.title: Show stash contents
commands.description: Displays the actual code changes stored in a stash entry.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'stash@{0}' with the desired stash reference and run the command inside the repository.
commands.whenToUse: When you want to inspect a stash before restoring it.
commands.tip: Reviewing a stash first helps avoid applying the wrong changes.

commands.title: Pop latest stash
commands.description: Restores the most recent stash and removes it from the stash list.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository when you are ready to continue working on the stashed changes.
commands.whenToUse: After switching back to the correct branch or finishing an interruption.
commands.tip: Resolve any merge conflicts before continuing development.

commands.title: Apply specific stash
commands.description: Restores a specific stash without deleting it from the stash list.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'stash@{1}' with the desired stash reference and run the command inside the repository.
commands.whenToUse: When the same stash may need to be applied more than once or kept for later use.
commands.tip: Use 'git stash list' to find the correct stash reference.

commands.title: Drop a stash
commands.description: Removes a specific stash entry permanently.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'stash@{0}' with the target stash reference and run the command inside the repository.
commands.whenToUse: After confirming that the stashed work is no longer needed.
commands.tip: Inspect the stash before deleting it because recovering dropped stashes can be difficult.

commands.title: Clear all stashes
commands.description: Deletes every stash entry from the repository.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository after verifying that none of the saved stashes are needed.
commands.whenToUse: When cleaning up old or obsolete stash entries.
commands.tip: Use 'git stash list' first to review what will be removed.

commands.title: Create annotated tag
commands.description: Creates a version tag with metadata such as author, date, and a message.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository and replace the version and message with your release information.
commands.whenToUse: When publishing official releases or marking important milestones.
commands.tip: Annotated tags are the preferred choice for production releases.

commands.title: Create lightweight tag
commands.description: Creates a simple tag that points to the current commit.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository and replace the version with the desired tag name.
commands.whenToUse: For temporary markers or informal version references.
commands.tip: Use annotated tags for release versions that require metadata.

commands.title: Tag a past commit
commands.description: Adds a tag to a specific commit instead of the current one.
commands.howToUse: Replace the version, message, and commit hash with the values you want to use.
commands.whenToUse: When you forgot to tag an important commit at the time it was created.
commands.tip: Use 'git log --oneline' to locate the commit hash before tagging.

commands.title: List all tags
commands.description: Displays every tag available in the repository.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the project folder to view existing tags.
commands.whenToUse: Before creating, pushing, or reviewing release versions.
commands.tip: Consistent version naming makes tags easier to manage.

commands.title: Show tag details
commands.description: Displays information about a specific tag and the commit it references.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'v1.0.0' with the tag you want to inspect and run the command inside the repository.
commands.whenToUse: When reviewing release information or verifying a tag's target commit.
commands.tip: Annotated tags provide additional metadata compared to lightweight tags.

commands.title: Push a tag
commands.description: Uploads a specific tag to the remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'v1.0.0' with the tag name and run the command after creating the tag locally.
commands.whenToUse: After preparing a release that should be available on GitHub or another remote.
commands.tip: Tags are not included in a normal push and must be pushed separately.

commands.title: Push all tags
commands.description: Uploads all local tags to the remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository when you want to synchronize every local tag with the remote.
commands.whenToUse: When multiple tags have been created and need to be published together.
commands.tip: Review your tags with 'git tag -l' before pushing them.

commands.title: Delete a local tag
commands.description: Removes a tag from your local repository without affecting the remote version.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository and replace 'v1.0.0' with the tag you want to remove.
commands.whenToUse: When a tag was created incorrectly or is no longer needed locally.
commands.tip: Deleting a local tag does not remove the same tag from GitHub or other remotes.

commands.title: Delete a remote tag
commands.description: Removes a tag from the remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'v1.0.0' with the tag name and run the command after confirming the tag should be removed.
commands.whenToUse: When a release tag or milestone tag was pushed by mistake.
commands.tip: Consider notifying collaborators before deleting shared tags.

commands.title: Ignore node_modules
commands.description: Adds the node_modules directory to .gitignore to prevent dependencies from being tracked.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the project root where the .gitignore file exists.
commands.whenToUse: At the beginning of any Node.js or JavaScript project.
commands.tip: Never commit node_modules. Dependencies should be recreated with package.json and package-lock.json.

commands.title: Ignore environment files
commands.description: Prevents environment files containing secrets from being committed.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the project root to add '.env' to the .gitignore file.
commands.whenToUse: Whenever your project uses API keys, database credentials, or other sensitive values.
commands.tip: If a .env file has already been committed, remove it from Git tracking immediately.

commands.title: Ignore build outputs
commands.description: Adds common build directories to .gitignore.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the project root to append the directories to the existing .gitignore file.
commands.whenToUse: For projects that generate build artifacts, such as React or Next.js applications.
commands.tip: Generated files should be rebuilt, not version-controlled.

commands.title: Ignore OS files
commands.description: Prevents operating system and editor temporary files from being tracked.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the project root to add common junk files to .gitignore.
commands.whenToUse: At the start of a new repository.
commands.tip: Ignoring these files keeps commits cleaner and avoids unnecessary changes.

commands.title: Ignore log files
commands.description: Prevents log files and log directories from being tracked by Git.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the project root to append the rules to .gitignore.
commands.whenToUse: For applications that generate logs during development or production.
commands.tip: Large log files can clutter repositories and increase repository size unnecessarily.

commands.title: Check why a file is ignored
commands.description: Shows which .gitignore rule is causing a file to be ignored.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'path/to/file' with the file you want to inspect and run the command inside the repository.
commands.whenToUse: When a file you expect Git to track is being ignored unexpectedly.
commands.tip: The output includes both the matching rule and the file responsible for it.

commands.title: Stop tracking ignored file
commands.code: git rm --cached path/to/file && git commit -m "chore: remove tracked file"
commands.description: Removes a file from Git tracking while keeping it on disk.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'path/to/file' with the target file and ensure it is already listed in .gitignore before running the command.
commands.whenToUse: When a file that should be ignored has already been committed.
commands.tip: The file remains on your device but will no longer be tracked by Git.

commands.title: Global gitignore
commands.description: Configures a global ignore file that applies to every repository on the device.
commands.howToUse: Run once and add your commonly ignored files to ~/.gitignore_global.
commands.whenToUse: When you want the same ignore rules across all projects.
commands.tip: Useful for ignoring OS-specific files such as .DS_Store and Thumbs.db everywhere.

commands.title: Sync fork with upstream
commands.code: git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main && git push
commands.description: Updates your fork with the latest changes from the original repository.
commands.howToUse: Run inside your forked repository after configuring the upstream remote.
commands.whenToUse: Periodically to keep your fork aligned with the source project.
commands.tip: Resolve rebase conflicts carefully before pushing the updated branch.

commands.title: Create a PR-ready branch
commands.code: git switch -c fix/issue-42 && # make changes && git add . && git commit -m "fix: resolve issue #42" && git push -u origin HEAD
commands.description: Creates a branch, commits your work, and pushes it to the remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Replace the branch name and commit message, make your changes, then run the remaining commands from the project directory.
commands.whenToUse: When preparing a bug fix or feature for a Pull Request.
commands.tip: Use descriptive branch names and commit messages to make reviews easier.

commands.title: Create GitHub repo from Termux
commands.description: Connects a local repository to a GitHub repository created through the website.
commands.howToUse: Create the repository on GitHub without initializing it, copy the SSH URL, then add it as the origin remote and push your branch.
commands.whenToUse: When publishing a new local project to GitHub.
commands.tip: Using SSH avoids entering credentials each time you push.

commands.title: Create personal access token
commands.code: # GitHub → Settings → Developer Settings → Tokens → Generate
commands.description: Generates a Personal Access Token for authenticating Git operations over HTTPS.
commands.howToUse: Create the token from GitHub settings, grant the required permissions, and use the token instead of your password when prompted.
commands.whenToUse: When using HTTPS authentication for GitHub repositories.
commands.tip: Store the token securely because GitHub only shows it once.

commands.title: Find the bad commit (bisect)
commands.code: git bisect start && git bisect bad && git bisect good abc1234
commands.description: Uses binary search to identify the commit that introduced a bug.
commands.howToUse: Start the bisect process, mark the current commit as bad, specify a known good commit, test each commit Git checks out, and finish with 'git bisect reset' when done.
commands.whenToUse: When a bug appears and you need to determine which commit introduced the problem.
commands.tip: The fewer commits between the good and bad states, the faster Git can locate the culprit.

commands.title: Worktree (work on 2 branches)
commands.description: Creates another working directory with a different branch checked out.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository to create a separate folder for the specified branch.
commands.whenToUse: When you need to work on a hotfix without interrupting ongoing feature development.
commands.tip: Worktrees are useful for avoiding repeated branch switching.

commands.title: Sparse checkout
commands.code: git sparse-checkout init --cone && git sparse-checkout set src docs
commands.description: Checks out only selected directories from a repository.
commands.howToUse: Initialize sparse checkout and specify the folders you want available locally.
commands.whenToUse: When working with large repositories where you only need a subset of files.
commands.tip: Sparse checkout can significantly reduce disk usage and improve performance.

commands.title: Add a submodule
commands.description: Adds another Git repository as a dependency inside the current repository.
commands.howToUse: Replace the repository URL and destination path, then run the command from the project root.
commands.whenToUse: When your project depends on external source code maintained in a separate repository.
commands.tip: Remember to initialize and update submodules after cloning the project.

commands.title: Git LFS (large files)
commands.code: git lfs install && git lfs track "*.psd"
commands.description: Configures Git Large File Storage for managing large binary files.
commands.howToUse: Install Git LFS, then specify the file patterns you want Git LFS to manage.
commands.whenToUse: When storing large assets such as images, videos, or design files.
commands.tip: Using Git LFS prevents large files from bloating repository history.

commands.title: Archive a branch
commands.description: Creates a ZIP archive of a branch without including Git history.
commands.howToUse: Replace the output filename and branch name, then run the command inside the repository.
commands.whenToUse: When sharing source code or preparing files for deployment.
commands.tip: The archive contains only the files from the selected branch.

commands.title: Count lines of code
commands.description: Counts the total number of lines across tracked files.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository to calculate line counts for all tracked files.
commands.whenToUse: When estimating project size or reviewing codebase statistics.
commands.tip: Only files tracked by Git are included in the count.

commands.title: Garbage collect
commands.description: Optimizes repository storage and removes unnecessary objects.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository when maintenance or cleanup is needed.
commands.whenToUse: When a repository becomes slow or after rewriting history and removing large files.
commands.tip: The aggressive option may take some time on large repositories.

commands.title: Daily workflow (complete)
commands.code: git pull && git add . && git commit -m "feat: your message" && git push
commands.description: Performs the typical pull, stage, commit, and push workflow.
commands.howToUse: Run each step from the project directory and replace the commit message with a meaningful description.
commands.whenToUse: During everyday development when saving and publishing changes.
commands.tip: Review your changes with 'git status' before running 'git add .' to avoid committing unwanted files.

commands.title: New feature workflow
commands.code: git switch -c feature/name && # code && git add . && git commit -m "feat: description" && git push -u origin HEAD
commands.description: Creates a branch and prepares a new feature for collaboration.
commands.howToUse: Replace the branch name and commit message, make your changes, then push the branch to the remote repository.
commands.whenToUse: Whenever starting a new feature or enhancement.
commands.tip: Creating a dedicated branch keeps feature work isolated from the main branch.

commands.title: Oops, undo last commit
commands.description: Removes the latest commit while preserving all changes in the staging area.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository immediately after an incorrect commit.
commands.whenToUse: When you need to adjust the last commit without losing your work.
commands.tip: You can edit files or amend the commit before committing again.

commands.title: What just happened?
commands.description: Displays the most recent commits in a compact format.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository to view the last ten commits.
commands.whenToUse: When checking recent changes or investigating repository history.
commands.tip: Increase the number to see more commits.

commands.title: Am I on the right branch?
commands.description: Shows the name of the currently checked-out branch.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository before committing or pushing changes.
commands.whenToUse: When verifying that you are working on the correct branch.
commands.tip: Checking the branch first helps prevent accidental commits to the wrong branch.

commands.title: What files did I change?
commands.description: Displays changed files using a concise status format.
commands.howToUse: Run inside the repository to quickly review modified, added, deleted, and untracked files.
commands.whenToUse: When you need a quick overview of your working directory.
commands.tip: The letters in the output indicate the type of change for each file.

commands.title: Clone a repository
commands.description: Downloads a complete copy of a remote repository.
commands.howToUse: Replace 'username/repo' with the repository path and run the command from the directory where you want the project created.
commands.whenToUse: Whenever you want to work on an existing GitHub repository.
commands.tip: SSH URLs are recommended if you have SSH keys configured.

commands.title: Clone a repo (HTTPS)
commands.description: Downloads a complete copy of a remote repository including full history, branches, and files.
commands.howToUse: Navigate to your projects folder in Termux, copy the HTTPS URL from GitHub, then run the command with the repo URL.
commands.whenToUse: When starting work on an existing GitHub project or contributing to open-source codebases.
commands.tip: HTTPS is easier for beginners but may require authentication tokens for pushes.

commands.title: Clone a repo (SSH)
commands.description: Clones a repository using SSH authentication without requiring passwords.
commands.howToUse: Ensure SSH keys are configured on GitHub, then run the command with the SSH repo URL.
commands.whenToUse: When you have SSH keys set up and want faster, passwordless Git operations.
commands.tip: SSH is the recommended method for long-term development workflows.

commands.title: Clone into specific folder
commands.description: Clones a repository into a custom directory name instead of the default repo name.
